These exercises accompany Part 3. They build on the phase-plane tools developed
throughout: nullclines and steady states ([Part 3A](03a-nullclines.qmd),
[Part 3B](03b-steady-states-2d.qmd)), bifurcation diagrams
([Part 3E](03e-bifurcation-2d.qmd)), and numerical continuation
([Part 2F](../02-odes/02f-bifurcation-curves.qmd)). Work in whichever language you
prefer; the R and Python routines from the earlier chapters carry over.

## 3I.1 Numerical continuation for a 2D bifurcation

Reproduce the bifurcation curves of [Part 3E](03e-bifurcation-2d.qmd) using
numerical continuation instead of separation of variables. The steady states of a
two-variable system with a control parameter $\lambda$ trace a curve satisfying

\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
f_X(X, Y, \lambda) = 0 \\
f_Y(X, Y, \lambda) = 0
\end{cases} \tag{1}
\end{equation}

two equations in three unknowns, so the solution set is a one-dimensional curve.
Differentiating with respect to $X$, $Y$, and $\lambda$ gives

$$
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial f_X}{\partial X}\Delta X + \dfrac{\partial f_X}{\partial Y}\Delta Y + \dfrac{\partial f_X}{\partial \lambda}\Delta \lambda = 0 \\[2mm]
\dfrac{\partial f_Y}{\partial X}\Delta X + \dfrac{\partial f_Y}{\partial Y}\Delta Y + \dfrac{\partial f_Y}{\partial \lambda}\Delta \lambda = 0
\end{cases}
$$

In matrix form, with the Jacobian $\mathbf{J}$, the state increment
$\Delta\mathbf{X} = (\Delta X, \Delta Y)^\top$, and $\mathbf{f} = (f_X, f_Y)^\top$,

$$ \mathbf{J}\,\Delta\mathbf{X} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \lambda}\,\Delta\lambda = 0 . \tag{2} $$

Solving for the tangent of the bifurcation curve,

$$ \frac{d\mathbf{X}}{d\lambda} = -\mathbf{J}^{-1}\frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \lambda} . \tag{3} $$

Equation (3) generalizes the one-variable continuation of
[Part 2E](../02-odes/02e-bifurcation.qmd) to two variables. Implement it (a
predictor step along $d\mathbf{X}/d\lambda$ followed by a Newton correction back
onto Equation (1)) and recover the saddle-node and pitchfork diagrams of
[Part 3E](03e-bifurcation-2d.qmd).

## 3I.2 A flip-flop gene circuit

Two transcription factors $X$ and $Y$: $X$ activates $Y$, and $Y$ inhibits $X$.

![](images/03i/flip-flop.png){width=30% fig-align="center"}

The rate equations are

\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{dX}{dt} = g_{X0} + g_{X1}\dfrac{1}{1 + (Y/Y_0)^{n_Y}} - k_X X \\[2mm]
\dfrac{dY}{dt} = g_{Y0} + g_{Y1}\dfrac{(X/X_0)^{n_X}}{1 + (X/X_0)^{n_X}} - k_Y Y
\end{cases} \tag{4}
\end{equation}

Explore the system with phase-plane analysis.

**(1)** How many steady states can the circuit have?

**(2)** What is the stability of each steady state?

## 3I.3 A toggle switch with self-activating genes

Two transcription factors $X$ and $Y$: each inhibits the other and activates
itself.

![](images/03i/self-activating-toggle.png){width=30% fig-align="center"}

The rate equations are

\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{dX}{dt} = \left(g_{X0} + g_{X1}\dfrac{(X/X_{0X})^{n_{XX}}}{1 + (X/X_{0X})^{n_{XX}}}\right)\dfrac{1}{1 + (Y/Y_{0X})^{n_{YX}}} - k_X X \\[2mm]
\dfrac{dY}{dt} = \left(g_{Y0} + g_{Y1}\dfrac{(Y/Y_{0Y})^{n_{YY}}}{1 + (Y/Y_{0Y})^{n_{YY}}}\right)\dfrac{1}{1 + (X/X_{0Y})^{n_{XY}}} - k_Y Y
\end{cases} \tag{5}
\end{equation}

All of $g_{X0}, g_{X1}, X_{0X}, Y_{0Y}, Y_{0X}, X_{0Y}, n_{XX}, n_{YX}, n_{YY},
n_{XY}, k_X, k_Y$ are parameters. Using any of the numerical methods from Part 3,
find a parameter set for which the system has **five** steady states, three of
them stable. For that case, choose sensible axis ranges and grid spacing, then

**(1)** plot the vector field (vectors or unit vectors; pick a scaling that keeps
the plot legible);

**(2)** plot the nullclines;

**(3)** locate the steady states numerically;

**(4)** classify each steady state from the eigenvalues of its Jacobian;

**(5)** plot a bifurcation diagram of the steady-state $X$ against the control
parameter $k_X$.

## 3I.4 The FitzHugh-Nagumo model

The FitzHugh-Nagumo model is a two-variable reduction of the Hodgkin-Huxley
neuron, a standard model of an excitable system
[@fitzhugh1961impulses; @nagumo1962active]:

\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{dv}{dt} = v - \dfrac{v^3}{3} - w + I \\[2mm]
\dfrac{dw}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{\tau}(v + a - bw)
\end{cases} \tag{6}
\end{equation}

where $v$ is the membrane potential, $w$ a recovery variable, $I$ the input
current, $\tau$ a time constant, and $a, b$ parameters. Use $a = 0.7$, $b = 0.8$,
$\tau = 12.5$.

**(1)** Implement the model with an ODE solver (e.g. RK4) and explore how changing
$I$ affects the dynamics.

**(2)** For $I = 0.5$, draw the phase plane: nullclines, vector field, and the
steady states.

**(3)** Compute bifurcation diagrams with $I$ as the control parameter over
$(-1.5, 1.5)$. For the vertical axis, try both the steady-state values of $v$ (or
$w$) and the maximum and minimum of $v$ (or $w$) along a trajectory.

## 3I.5 The spruce budworm model revisited

We revisit the spruce budworm [@ludwig1978qualitative] (see also
[Part 2F](../02-odes/02f-bifurcation-curves.qmd)), now as two interacting
populations: the budworms (prey, $W$) and their predators ($P$),

\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{dW}{dt} = rW\left(1 - \dfrac{W}{K}\right) - aWP \\[2mm]
\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -kP + bWP
\end{cases} \tag{7}
\end{equation}

with intrinsic growth rate $r$, carrying capacity $K$, predation rate $a$,
predator death rate $k$, and predator growth rate $b$. Use $r = 0.1$, $K = 1$,
$a = 0.02$, $k = 0.2$, $b = 0.01$.

**(1)** Implement the model with an ODE solver and simulate the populations from
several initial conditions. Describe the behavior of $W$ and $P$.

**(2)** Do a phase-plane analysis: nullclines, vector field, and steady states.

**(3)** Explore the bifurcation diagram of the budworm population $W$ as $a$ is
varied.

## 3I.6 A chaotic system

The Lorenz system [@lorenz1963deterministic] is a three-variable system famous for
its chaotic dynamics,

\begin{equation}
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \sigma (y - x) \\[2mm]
\dfrac{dy}{dt} = x (\rho - z) - y \\[2mm]
\dfrac{dz}{dt} = xy - \beta z
\end{cases} \tag{8}
\end{equation}

with parameters $\sigma$, $\rho$, and $\beta$. Study how its behavior changes as
the parameters vary.

**(1)** Implement the ODEs for simulation.

**(2)** Fix $\sigma = 10$ and $\beta = 8/3$, and take $\rho$ as the control
parameter. For each $\rho$ from $20$ to $400$, simulate for a duration of $1000$
time units and plot the final $z$ levels against $\rho$.

**(3)** From the diagram, identify regions of stability, bifurcation points, and
transitions as $\rho$ is varied.
